strengths: Curates a very large multi-institutional ultrasound dataset (208,941 cases, 1.47M images, 15 hospitals, 7 organ systems), which if released would be a valuable resource for the community.

Proposes a reasonably motivated Dual-path MoE design (frozen copy of original FFN as an anchor plus shared/routed active experts) intended to inject domain knowledge while mitigating catastrophic forgetting of general multimodal ability.

Evaluation spans three clinically relevant tasks (report generation, diagnosis, VQA) across seven anatomical regions with multiple standard NLG metrics, and includes ablations on shared expert usage, Top-K routing, and expert count that show generally consistent trends.

Provides interpretability analyses (expert routing distributions by modality/layer, Grad-CAM visualizations) and qualitative case studies that give some insight into model behavior beyond aggregate scores.
weaknesses: No ethics/IRB statement or discussion of patient consent and de-identification despite using multi-hospital clinical ultrasound images and reports; this is a serious omission for a paper built entirely on real patient data.

Reported headline numbers in the abstract (+10.15 BLEU-1, +4.77 ROUGE-1 over Qwen2-VL) do not match Table 2's actual gap between EchoVLM and Qwen2-VL (which is much larger, ~47 BLEU-1 points); the quoted numbers instead correspond to the 0-expert vs 4-expert ablation in Table 7, creating a confusing and seemingly incorrect central claim.

Baseline comparisons are not clearly controlled: it is unclear whether 'LLaVA-OneVision-Ultrasound' and 'Qwen2-VL-Ultrasound' were fine-tuned with the same two-stage protocol, same amount of compute, and same data as EchoVLM, and EchoVLM (11B) is compared against 7B fine-tuned baselines, confounding architecture/MoE contribution with model size.

Evaluation relies solely on surface-level NLG metrics (BLEU, ROUGE, METEOR, BERTScore); no clinical correctness/factuality assessment, expert rating of generated reports, or hallucination analysis is provided, which is critical for a medical report-generation system intended for diagnostic support.

Performance is inconsistent: EchoVLM underperforms both generic and specialized baselines on vessel report generation and diagnosis, and wins only 16/35 metric-anatomy combinations on VQA, undermining the 'universal' framing and the claim of consistent superiority.

Reproducibility is limited in practice: the core clinical dataset (hospital-sourced images/reports) is proprietary and unlikely to be releasable, so independent verification of the central empirical claims is not feasible even if code/weights are shared.

The instruction-tuning data generation pipeline relies heavily on LLM-generated QA pairs with only 5% batch-level expert sampling for validation, which is a fairly weak quality-control mechanism for safety-critical medical content.

The technical contribution (MoE with a frozen anchor FFN, shared expert, LoRA-tuned routed experts) is an incremental combination of established techniques (MoE, LoRA) rather than a novel algorithmic advance, and the paper does not compare against other ultrasound- or medical-specific VLMs beyond generic baselines.
No variance/significance reporting across runs or statistical testing of the differences shown in tables; single-run results are used throughout including in ablations.

strengths: Curates a very large, multi-institutional (15 hospitals), multi-organ (7 anatomical systems) ultrasound dataset (208,941 cases, 1.47M key-frame images) and a 1.8M-pair instruction-tuning corpus via an expert-validated few-shot generation pipeline with deduplication and dual (AI + expert) verification, which is a substantial resource contribution to a domain with limited multimodal data.

Proposes a technically reasonable Dual-path MoE design (frozen static expert + shared expert + sparsely-routed experts) combined with a two-stage (parameter-isolated pretraining + LoRA cooperative fine-tuning) strategy intended to inject domain knowledge while mitigating catastrophic forgetting; the design is clearly motivated and ablated.

Extensive empirical evaluation across three tasks (report generation, diagnosis, VQA), seven anatomical systems, and 12 baseline VLMs (including recent medical VLMs like Lingshu, MedGemma, HuatuoGPT-Vision), supplemented with entity-level clinical metrics, OOD generalization tests on an external public dataset, expert routing/load-balancing analysis, Grad-CAM visualizations, and qualitative case studies — a commendable breadth of analysis for an applied systems paper.
Ablations (shared expert, Top-k routing, number of experts) are systematic and provide some insight into design choices and compute/performance trade-offs.
weaknesses: The central clinical-utility claims rest almost entirely on automated NLG metrics (BLEU/ROUGE/METEOR/BERTScore) and an automated entity extractor; despite the paper's own acknowledgment that such metrics correlate imperfectly with clinical correctness, no human/radiologist evaluation of generated reports, diagnoses, or VQA answers is reported, which is a significant gap for a paper aiming at 'clinical translation.'

Performance gains are not uniform: EchoVLM underperforms strong baselines (e.g., Lingshu) on multiple VQA metrics and on the vessel/vascular category across tasks, and the shared-expert ablation shows a negative effect on VQA BLEU-1/METEOR, complicating the paper's largely positive framing of 'consistent' improvements.

Reproducibility is questionable: the abstract's code/weights link is truncated/missing, the training data are private hospital data not clearly releasable, and no clear statement is given about what (if anything) will actually be publicly available, undermining the 'first open-source' framing.

No statistical significance testing or variance/multiple-run reporting is provided for the many pairwise comparisons across 12 models × 7 systems × 5 metrics × 3 tasks, so the reliability of small performance differences (often <1-2 points) is unclear.

Ethical/privacy handling is only briefly described (IRB approval, regex-based desensitization) without detail on demographic representativeness, potential bias across hospitals/populations, or safeguards for clinical deployment risk, which is important given the sensitive medical application.

The interpretation of some ablations (e.g., 4 vs 6 experts being framed as 'optimal trade-off' based on marginal gains and training-time cost) and some SOTA claims in the text are somewhat selectively emphasized despite mixed results in the underlying tables.
Related work and framing are largely descriptive rather than sharply differentiating EchoVLM's architectural novelty from prior general-purpose MoE-VLM or medical VLM knowledge-injection approaches.

strengths: Introduces and releases (claimed) the largest multi-organ ultrasound dataset to date (208,941 cases, 1.47M key-frame images, 15 hospitals, 7 anatomical systems, >100 disease/finding categories), which is a substantial resource contribution to the community if truly released.

Develops a non-trivial expert-validated multi-task instruction-generation pipeline (21 expert templates, dual AI+human verification, deduplication via ROUGE-L/Simhash) producing 1.8M instruction pairs, with reasonably detailed documentation in the appendix (prompts, filtering criteria).

Extensive experimental coverage: three tasks (report generation, diagnosis, VQA), 12 baseline VLMs (general and medical-specific), seven anatomical systems, and both surface-level (BLEU/ROUGE/METEOR/BERTScore) and fine-grained entity-level evaluation, which partially compensates for the known weaknesses of n-gram metrics in clinical text.
Reasonably thorough ablation studies (shared expert, Top-1 vs Top-2 routing, number of experts vs. training cost trade-off) that support the design choices of the Dual-path MoE.

Includes an out-of-distribution evaluation on an external public dataset (Li et al. 2024b) to probe generalization, plus routing-distribution analysis and Grad-CAM visualizations for interpretability.

Two-stage training strategy (frozen-base MoE pretraining + LoRA cooperative fine-tuning) is a sensible, well-motivated approach to mitigating catastrophic forgetting while injecting domain knowledge, and baselines are reportedly trained under a comparable full-parameter fine-tuning paradigm for fairer comparison.
weaknesses: No human/clinical expert evaluation of the actual generated reports, diagnoses, or VQA answers in the final test results — all reported numbers rely on automated metrics (BLEU/ROUGE/BERTScore) and an automated entity extractor; expert validation was only applied during instruction-data curation, not to model outputs, which is a significant gap for a paper making clinical-translation claims.

Reliance on n-gram/embedding metrics for medical report quality is a well-known limitation; while entity-level metrics are added, these depend on an unvalidated "clinically validated extractor" whose own accuracy is not reported, limiting confidence in this supplementary evidence.

Some overclaiming/inconsistency: the introduction describes EchoVLM as having "tens of billions of parameters," while the actual models are 3B/11B, and the abstract states 10B — this inflated framing undercuts precision of the central claims.

No statistical significance testing or repeated runs are reported for any comparison (baselines, ablations), so it is unclear whether reported gains (e.g., 1–5 point differences) are robust versus noise from a single training/evaluation run.

Reproducibility is only partially supported: source code/weight availability is referenced but the actual link/footnote is missing in the manuscript text, and the multi-hospital clinical dataset itself likely cannot be fully released due to patient privacy, limiting independent verification of the central dataset-scale claims.

The core architectural novelty (frozen anchor FFN + shared expert + sparsely-routed experts) is an incremental combination of existing MoE design patterns (e.g., shared/routed expert splits and frozen backbones seen in prior MoE-LLM work); the primary contribution is more the domain application and data scale than a fundamentally new method.

VQA results are mixed/weaker than competitors (e.g., underperforming Lingshu on several metrics, occasional negative deltas in ablations for BLEU-1/METEOR), and vascular-system performance is notably poor, both acknowledged only briefly as limitations without deeper analysis or mitigation in the main study.

Presentation issues: extremely dense tables/figures, some grammatically informal ablation description text (Section 4.3.3 reads like unedited notes), and truncated abstract text ("available a") suggest the manuscript needs more careful proofreading before publication.
